Studies have demonstrated a strong correlation between hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA levels and HCV core antigen in liver biopsies of patients with chronic hepatitis C undergoing liver transplantation. This relationship was first reported in 1993 in the journal Hepatology. 2. 3. Wu (2009) investigated the detection of HCV antigens in hemodialysis patients, emphasizing the importance of antigen testing in non-blood specimens. 4. Xie et al. (2011) developed a magnetic microparticle-based immunoassay for detecting HCV NS3 antigen, which showed promise in improving diagnostic accuracy. 5. Xie and colleagues (2009) analyzed the clinical application of an ELISA-based method for detecting HCV NS3 antigen in human serum, providing insights into its diagnostic potential. 6. Yagci and Padalko (2012) compared the Monolisa HCV Ag/Ab Ultra assay with two anti-HCV assays for detecting HCV infection in hospital settings, demonstrating its diagnostic reliability. 7. Yan et al. (2000) explored the expression of HCV antigens and viral replication in extrahepatic tissues, suggesting that HCV may infect tissues beyond the liver. 8. Yang and Wei (2014) identified factors influencing the utility of HCV core antigen assays, presenting their findings at the Hepatology International conference. 9. Reyes-Mendez et al. (2014) compared two diagnostic algorithms for identifying HCV viremia using a novel HCV antigen test, highlighting its potential in clinical practice. 10. Studies have consistently shown that HCV core antigen levels correlate with HCV RNA levels and can predict sustained virologic response (SVR) to antiviral therapies, such as pegylated interferon and ribavirin. 11. Research has also demonstrated the clinical utility of HCV core antigen assays in monitoring treatment response, particularly in patients with chronic HCV genotype 1 infection. 12. The use of dried blood spots (DBS) for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) testing has been systematically reviewed, showing acceptable diagnostic accuracy compared to venous blood samples. This method is particularly advantageous in low-resource settings due to its simplicity, reduced need for cold chain storage, and lower risk of contamination. 13. WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of improving HBV screening in high-prevalence, lowand middle-income countries. The use of DBS for serological and molecular testing is being considered to enhance access to and uptake of testing. 14. Studies have highlighted the need for operational research to evaluate the real-life accuracy of DBS testing under various environmental conditions, such as high humidity. 15. The diagnostic accuracy of DBS for HBsAg testing has been assessed through systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with findings supporting its use in decentralized settings where venous blood collection is challenging. 16. The development of novel assays, such as chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassays, has improved the sensitivity and specificity of HCV core antigen detection, enabling earlier and more accurate monitoring of treatment response. 17. Research continues to explore the predictive value of HCV core antigen testing for treatment outcomes, with studies demonstrating its ability to forecast virologic response and guide therapeutic decisions. 18. The integration of HCV core antigen testing into diagnostic algorithms has been proposed as a cost-effective alternative to nucleic acid testing, particularly in resource-limited settings. 19. The clinical relevance of HCV core antigen levels as a marker of infection and response to therapy has been validated in multiple studies, underscoring its role in the management of chronic hepatitis C. 20. The use of DBS for HBV and HCV testing is gaining traction as a practical solution for expanding diagnostic capabilities in underserved regions, with ongoing research aimed at optimizing its implementation and accuracy.
